summary: An April 1st joke RFC written in mock archaic English. It supplies a collection of ASCII art creatures for authors to reuse in documents, with a tongue-in-cheek history of ASCII. It is humor, not a protocol.

eli5.summary: A funny old-style book of pictures drawn with keyboard letters, like a dragon made from dashes and slashes.

subtitle: ASCII art creatures and structures for reuse in IETF documents

tldr.problem: IETF documents have historically been plain text with no visual embellishment. Authors sometimes want to include ASCII art but have no repository of tested designs to reuse.
tldr.mechanism: This April 1st RFC supplies a collection of ASCII art renderings of mythical beasts, real creatures, and structures, written in mock-archaic English, that authors can copy into their documents.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st humor document, not a protocol specification. It showcases ASCII art while poking fun at RFC conventions and the history of IETF documentation.

today: RFC 8140 is an April 1st humor document published in the Independent Submission stream. It is not a protocol specification and should not be used as such. It exemplifies the RFC Series' tradition of publishing humor and satire on April 1st.

sections.title: The Premise
sections.content:
This is an April 1st humor RFC written in deliberately archaic English that pretends ASCII and the Courier New font were discovered by Gutenberg. The document supplies ASCII art renderings of various creatures and structures that RFC authors might want to reuse in their documents.

The tone is mock-scholarly, treating ASCII art as a serious catalog of 'sightings' of legendary and real creatures. The RFC references other humorous RFCs like RFC 1925 (Thrusted Pigs) and RFC 1149 (IP over Avian Carriers).
sections.eli5: Someone wrote a funny book that pretends ASCII art is an ancient art form and provides a bunch of examples.

sections.title: The Menagerie
sections.content:
The RFC organizes ASCII art into categories: Beasts of the Land (Trolls and Unicorns), Creatures of the Deep (Loch Ness Monster, Swordfish), Spirits of the Air (Vampires and Avian Carriers), and Man-Made Structures (Bauhaus geometric designs and a Gingerbread House).

The descriptions are humorous and topical. The Troll section notes that trolls 'feed on passing goats and cookies' and should 'never be fed.' The Unicorn section notes that 'Unicorns can only be captured by the pure of heart who have never operated a real network.' The Avian Carriers section references RFC 1149's IP-over-pigeons joke.
sections.eli5: It has drawings of trolls, unicorns, monsters, bats, buildings, and birds, all made from keyboard characters.

sections.title: For Amusement Only
sections.content:
The RFC includes elaborate mock-serious sections on Manageability Considerations, Morality Considerations (discussing misuse by the depraved, misguided, and corporations), and Security Considerations that show ASCII art renderings of locks and mirrors. These are entirely humorous.

The document is a product of the Independent Submission stream, meaning it is not an IETF standard and is published purely for entertainment. It exemplifies the RFC Series' tradition of April 1st humor while staying true to the ASCII character set that has been central to IETF documentation.
sections.eli5: There are funny sections about safety and security that are really just more ASCII art pictures.
